# TLS certificate or host name verification disabled (Java)

`qualor:java/tls-verification-disabled` · Issue · Severity: High · [CWE-295](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/295.html) · OWASP Top 10: [A07:2025 Authentication Failures](https://top10.owasp.org/2025/A07_2025-Authentication_Failures/), [A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures](https://top10.owasp.org/2021/A07_2021-Identification_and_Authentication_Failures/)

## What it finds

<!-- begin: what-it-finds -->
TLS client checks that accept anything (JSSE, `javax.net.ssl`):

- a `checkServerTrusted` method of an `X509TrustManager` or `X509ExtendedTrustManager` that
  returns without checking the server's certificate chain: an empty body, one that only logs, or
  one that checks a certificate's dates or signature but catches the failure;
- a `HostnameVerifier` that returns `true` whatever the host: a `verify` method or a lambda given
  to `setHostnameVerifier` / `setDefaultHostnameVerifier`, assigned to a `HostnameVerifier`
  variable or cast to one.

A trust manager that throws `CertificateException`, delegates to another trust manager or hands
the chain, a copy of it or one of its certificates to a check of its own, and a verifier that returns `true` only under a condition, are
not reported. An empty `checkClientTrusted` is not reported either: a server calls it, and an
empty one only means that clients need no certificate. Test code is skipped: the `src/test/`
tree (also `src/testFixtures/`, `src/integrationTest/` and `src/intTest/`) and files whose
names end in `Test`, `Tests`, `TestCase`, `IT` or `ITCase`.
<!-- end: what-it-finds -->

## Why it matters

<!-- begin: why-it-matters -->
A trust manager that returns normally tells the JSSE that the chain is trusted, so the client
accepts any certificate, including one the attacker made a minute ago; a host name verifier that
returns `true` accepts a valid certificate issued for another site. Either way the connection is
still encrypted, but to whoever answers: anyone on the network path (a public Wi-Fi, a compromised
router, a proxy) can pose as the server, read the traffic and change it, including credentials
and tokens sent over it. Code like this is often added to reach a server with a self-signed
certificate during development and then ships.
<!-- end: why-it-matters -->

## Example

<!-- begin: example -->
**Noncompliant:** a trust-all manager to reach a server whose certificate comes from a private CA.

```java
package com.example.client;

import java.security.GeneralSecurityException;
import java.security.SecureRandom;
import java.security.cert.X509Certificate;
import javax.net.ssl.SSLContext;
import javax.net.ssl.TrustManager;
import javax.net.ssl.X509TrustManager;

public class Clients {
    public static SSLContext context() throws GeneralSecurityException {
        TrustManager[] trustAll = {
            new X509TrustManager() {
                public void checkClientTrusted(X509Certificate[] chain, String authType) {
                }

                public void checkServerTrusted(X509Certificate[] chain, String authType) {
                }

                public X509Certificate[] getAcceptedIssuers() {
                    return new X509Certificate[0];
                }
            }
        };
        SSLContext context = SSLContext.getInstance("TLS");
        context.init(null, trustAll, new SecureRandom());
        return context;
    }
}
```

**Compliant:** the private CA is in a trust store, and the default trust managers check against it.

```java
package com.example.client;

import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.InputStream;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.security.GeneralSecurityException;
import java.security.KeyStore;
import javax.net.ssl.SSLContext;
import javax.net.ssl.TrustManagerFactory;

public class Clients {
    public static SSLContext context(Path trustStore, char[] password) throws GeneralSecurityException, IOException {
        KeyStore store = KeyStore.getInstance("PKCS12");
        try (InputStream in = Files.newInputStream(trustStore)) {
            store.load(in, password);
        }
        TrustManagerFactory tmf = TrustManagerFactory.getInstance(TrustManagerFactory.getDefaultAlgorithm());
        tmf.init(store);
        SSLContext context = SSLContext.getInstance("TLS");
        context.init(null, tmf.getTrustManagers(), null);
        return context;
    }
}
```
<!-- end: example -->

## How to fix

<!-- begin: how-to-fix -->
- Remove the custom trust manager and host name verifier; the defaults check the certificate
  chain against the JDK's trust store and the host name against the certificate.
- To trust a private or self-signed CA, put its certificate in a trust store (a `KeyStore`), and
  build the `SSLContext` from a `TrustManagerFactory` initialised with it (or set
  `javax.net.ssl.trustStore`).
- If you must check certificates yourself (pinning, say), call the default trust manager first or
  compare what you need, and throw `CertificateException` when the check fails; in a
  `HostnameVerifier`, return the result of a real check, never a constant `true`.
<!-- end: how-to-fix -->

## Frameworks and APIs covered

- `javax.net.ssl`

## Known limits

<!-- begin: known-limits -->
- A `checkServerTrusted` that hands the chain (a copy, or one certificate of it) to any call
  counts as checking it, even a log message or a delegation to the default trust manager whose
  `CertificateException` is caught and only logged; one that throws anywhere counts too, even
  when its only throw is the `IllegalArgumentException` for a null or empty chain.
- A lambda counts as a host name verifier only where the code shows it is one (the JDK setters, a
  `HostnameVerifier` variable, a cast): one given to another library's builder, such as OkHttp's
  `hostnameVerifier`, is missed, and so are other libraries' own trust-all and no-op classes
  (Apache HttpClient's `NoopHostnameVerifier` and `TrustAllStrategy`).
- A trust-all manager given only to a server context (whose `checkServerTrusted` is never called)
  is still reported.
- Skipping test code by file name also skips a production class whose name ends in `Test` or `IT`.
<!-- end: known-limits -->

## Tests

The test file [`rules/java/tls/tls-verification-disabled.java`](../../../rules/java/tls/tls-verification-disabled.java) holds every case the rule reports or accepts:
lines marked `ruleid:` must be reported and lines marked `ok:` must not. The known limits are
marked `todoruleid:` (missed) and `todook:` (wrongly reported). `npm test` runs them with OpenGrep,
and checks the example above as well.

The rule: [`rules/java/tls/tls-verification-disabled.yml`](../../../rules/java/tls/tls-verification-disabled.yml), added in version 2026.10.2.
